newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Mongolians cast votes for president in tight race.
newsitem.headline: Mongolians cast votes for president in tight race.

text.p: Mongolians went to the polls on Sunday to vote for a new president in a race seen neck and neck between the nation's reformist leader and his challenger from the former communist party.
Some voters arrived on horseback while others walked from their felt tents on the outskirts of the capital to reach polling stations that opened early on Sunday.
A smiling President Punsalmaagiin Ochirbat cast his ballot and told his electorate this was a crucial contest for the once-communist nation.
"This is an important election," said the 55-year-old candidate of the Democratic Union Coalition as he and his wife Tsevelmaa greeted voters at a polling station in the capital.
"The person who is elected will lead us into the next century."

Ochirbat, who won Mongolia's first direct presidential election in June 1993 as an opposition candidate after he was dumped by the then-ruling party, the formerly communist Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party, has promised to continue his drive for democracy with another four-year term.
He has also pledged to eradicate poverty in a country where one in five Mongolians lives below the official poverty line with an income of $10 a month.

His main opponent, Natsagiin Bagabandi of the opposition Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party that had ruled for 75 years before their surprise election defeat last year, has campaigned for a slowdown of reforms that have created widespread economic dislocation.
Bagabandi, 47, has tried to appeal to those who have been left jobless as Mongolia moves from Stalinist central planning to a market economy.
"If I become president ... I will direct my efforts to make the state work like a real state," he said as he cast his vote.
A poll by the Sant Maaral Centre, a local think tank, gave the challenger 51 percent of the vote to the president's 44 percent.
Ochirbat's party controls parliament but the challenger, if elected, might be able to block legislation with a veto.

The 1.1 million eligible voters in this vast land wedged between Russia and China have a third candidate to choose from, Jambiin Gombojav, a parliament member running on the Mongolian Traditional United Party ticket. He is far behind the front-runners.
Poll officials said voter turnout would be high by Western standards but lower than the 90 percent seen in elections over the past few years.
"We expect about 70 percent of the 1,700 voters in this constituency to turn up," said Chagnaa a leader from Amgalan district on the outskirts of the city.
Results from across the sprawling land of the steppes were expected to be known on Monday at the earliest.
